mechanism: Increased hydrostatic pressure or decreased oncotic pressure in capillaries leads to fluid extravasation into the interstitial space. Impaired lymphatic drainage can also contribute.
visual_features: Pitting edema on the lower extremities
Swelling of the ankles and feet
clinical_context: Commonly seen in patients with heart failure, kidney disease, liver disease, venous insufficiency, or prolonged standing. Severity depends on the underlying cause.

mechanism: Formation of a blood clot in a deep vein, obstructing venous return and causing increased hydrostatic pressure distal to the thrombus, leading to edema.
clinical_context: Requires prompt diagnosis and treatment with anticoagulation to prevent pulmonary embolism. Risk factors include immobility, surgery, cancer, and hypercoagulable states.

mechanism: Bacterial infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissues, causing inflammation and fluid accumulation.
clinical_context: Typically caused by Streptococcus or Staphylococcus bacteria. Requires antibiotic treatment. Can progress to sepsis if untreated.

mechanism: Impairment of lymphatic drainage leading to accumulation of protein-rich fluid in the interstitial space. Can be primary (congenital) or secondary (e.g., due to surgery, radiation, infection).
visual_features: Stemmer's sign (inability to pinch the skin on the dorsum of the second toe)
clinical_context: Chronic condition requiring management with compression therapy and lymphatic drainage techniques. Can lead to recurrent infections and impaired function.

mechanism: Valvular incompetence in the veins of the lower extremities leads to venous hypertension, causing fluid leakage into the interstitial space and edema.
clinical_context: Common in patients with a history of DVT or prolonged standing. Management includes compression therapy, leg elevation, and wound care if ulcers are present.
